events.title: LLVM 1.0 released
events.summary: Chris Lattner released LLVM 1.0 on October 24, 2003 — an open compiler infrastructure with a reusable intermediate representation.
events.about: LLVM separates compilation into front ends (Clang, Rust), a portable IR, and back ends targeting x86, ARM, and more. Optimizations run on IR at compile, link, or even runtime. Swift, Rust, Julia, and Xcode all build on LLVM — teams add languages without rewriting code generation.

narrative.whyChosen: LLVM turned compilers into reusable libraries instead of monolithic GCC forks.
narrative.whyImportant: Its IR became the foundation for Clang, Swift, Rust, and modern language tooling.
narrative.problemSolved: Each new language or target meant forking a whole compiler; researchers needed modular optimization.

events.title: Xcode 1.0 released
events.summary: Apple shipped Xcode 1.0 on October 28, 2003 with Mac OS X Panther — integrating Project Builder into a modern Mac IDE.
events.about: Xcode became the mandatory toolchain for iOS and macOS development — Interface Builder, Instruments, lldb, and Swift support all live here. Every App Store binary is built with Xcode's compiler and signing pipeline.

narrative.whyChosen: Xcode is Apple's primary IDE for native platform development.
narrative.whyImportant: It unified Mac (and later iPhone) tooling under one environment.
narrative.problemSolved: Mac developers used fragmented Project Builder and external debuggers.
